blocks.text: Effect of Ligand Exchange on Stability Constant

blocks.md:
- The stability constants (*K*<sub>*stab*</sub>) of ligands are often given on a log<sub>10</sub> scale so that it becomes easier to compare them with each other
- Ligand exchange in a complex occurs to form a **more stable **complex with a larger *K*<sub>*stab*</sub>
- The stability constants can be used to explain the substitution of ligands in a copper complex

blocks.text: Ligand substitution in a Co(II) complex

blocks.md: - When excess ammonia is added to the [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> complex a **brown **solution is obtained

blocks.text: Ligand exchange of the [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> complex by ammonia

blocks.md: ***The chloride ligands are substituted by the ammonia ligands to form the more stable ammonia complex***** **
- The formation of the ammonia complex could be explained by comparing the stability of the chloride and ammonia ligands

blocks.text: Stability of chloride and ammonia ligands table

blocks.md:
- The stability constant of the ammonia ligand is greater than that of the chloride ligands
- The brown ammonia complex is therefore **more stable**
- As a result, the position of the equilibrium is shifted **to the right**

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
The numerical values for the stability constants, *K*<sub>*stab*</sub>, of three silver(I) complexes are given.

| **Silver(I) complex** | **Numerical value of *****K***<sub>***stab***</sub> |
|---|---|
| [Ag(S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> | 2.9 x 10<sup>13</sup> |
| [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>–</sup> | 5.3 x 10<sup>18</sup> |
| [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> | 1.6 x 10<sup>7</sup> |

An aqueous solution of Ag<sup>+</sup> is added to a solution containing equal concentrations of S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq), CN<sup>–</sup> (aq) and NH<sub>3</sub> (aq). The mixture is left to reach equilibrium.

Deduce the relative concentrations of [Ag(S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3–</sup>, [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>–</sup> and [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> present in the equilibrium mixture. Explain your answer.

**Answer**

- The highest concentration will be [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>–</sup>

  - This is because the *K*<sub>*stab*</sub> value for [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>–</sup> is the largest value 
  **OR**
  - [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>–</sup> is the most stable
- The lowest concentration will be [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>

  - This is because the *K*<sub>*stab*</sub> value for [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is the smallest value 
  **OR**
  - [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is the least stable
- An alternative explanation could be to state that higher *K*<sub>*stab*</sub> values form a more stable complex
